Hi @TruthGundlach,  

Here in the Netherlands, anyone with more than €30,000 in assets is considered wealthy.  

They get to pay a 36% tax on realized investment gains, including gains that just compensate for inflation. 

The government expects investors to keep track of every transaction themselves and report everything to the tax authorities.

And to keep things simple, our finance minister has proposed taxing directly held crypto and precious metals on unrealized gains instead. 

Give up direct ownership and buy an ETF-like product? You're back to being taxed on realized gains. 

Yes, the idea is to apply two tax systems to the same underlying asset.

All of this, of course, for the benefit of investors and a tax authority that has been struggling with overwhelming complexity and workloads for years.

Greetings from Rotterdam,  
Jeroen Blokland

text:
This is the new Tesla Roadster's fan and suction system, which the company filed a patent for in April 2025.

Sides skirts and front and rear skirts deploy under the battery pack, sucking the car down at ~2G. Because the skirts can move, they have some compliance, so they can deal with road bumps, road debris, etc. As the speed of the Roadster increases, the front and rear skirts retract to allow for air-flow (venturi effect) under the vehicle.

Tesla: "Our multi-mode fan and ground sealing system acts as a downforce generator, pulling air out from beneath the vehicle. This provides enough suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary. Powered fans and active wings maximize traction and cornering speeds in all conditions, achieving massive downforce at zero speed."

In their patent, Tesla said: "In the first mode, a complete set of skirts creates a fully sealed bounded region under the vehicle with central fans generating maximum downforce at low speeds on smooth surfaces. In the second mode, a subset of skirts (primarily side skirts) modifies the bounded region while all fans operate to provide downforce in dynamic driving conditions with uneven surfaces. The system includes a control mechanism to selectively deploy skirts and operate fans based on driving conditions, optimizing between maximum downforce at low speeds and improved performance over varying terrain at higher speeds."

text:
It’s becoming clear that MMTers have a worse understanding of reserve accounting than we thought. 

What matters is the total remittances, not IORB in isolation. And yes, in recent years the Fed has been operating at a loss, which has been net stimulative relative to the large positive remittances of prior years even though this income effect was offset by the tighter credit conditions that accompanied the rate hikes, which were a clear net drag and help explain why inflation fell after 2022.

What’s even more off-base about the idea that this might cause inflation is that the remittances matter in rate of change, not just levels. Saying “there’s $500B of new income because of IORB” doesn’t mean we got inflation from it. If you got $100B every year for 5 years you don’t get ongoing inflation because the rate of change isn’t changing. And in recent years the net interest impact has been improving as the Fed’s annual losses have shrunk substantially, meaning the incremental addition to the consolidated government deficit from this channel has been getting smaller, not larger. They have the direction of the flow backwards and this exercise explains why their theory of inflation has been so wrong in recent years.
